questions.body: Why is `mid = low + (high - low) / 2` preferred over `mid = (low + high) / 2` when implementing binary search?
questions.keyPoints: Prevents integer arithmetic overflow when low + high exceeds maximum 32-bit signed integer value.

options.text: It prevents integer overflow that occurs in languages with fixed-width integers (like Java and C++) when `low + high` exceeds `2^31 - 1`.
options.explanation: If `low` and `high` are large positive integers, `low + high` overflows into a negative number, resulting in an invalid negative array index. `low + (high - low) / 2` avoids the overflow completely.

options.text: It executes twice as fast on modern CPU architectures.
options.explanation: The operation takes identical CPU instruction cycles.

options.text: It automatically handles floating-point numbers.
options.explanation: It is an integer arithmetic overflow guard.

options.text: It handles unsorted arrays.
options.explanation: Binary search strictly requires a sorted or monotonic space.

questions.body: What characteristic must a problem exhibit to allow applying Binary Search on the Answer Space (e.g. 'Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days' or 'Koko Eating Bananas')?
questions.keyPoints: Monotonicity: if a condition is satisfied for value X, it is guaranteed to be satisfied for all values >= X (or <= X).

options.text: Monotonicity of the feasibility predicate: if a candidate answer `X` is valid, all values `> X` (or `< X`) are also guaranteed to be valid.
options.explanation: When a validation function `isValid(mid)` is monotonic (`F, F, F, T, T, T`), binary search can discard half the search space on each step, converging on the optimal answer in O(log(range) * checkCost).

options.text: The input array must already be sorted.
options.explanation: Binary search on answer space searches over a numeric range of values, not necessarily an input array.

options.text: The total number of elements must be a power of 2.
options.explanation: Binary search works on any integer range size.

options.text: The answer must always be a prime number.
options.explanation: Prime numbers have nothing to do with answer-space monotonicity.

questions.body: Under what condition does standard QuickSort with first-element pivot selection degrade to its worst-case O(N^2) time complexity?
questions.keyPoints: When the input array is already sorted or reverse-sorted.

options.text: When the array is already sorted or reverse-sorted, causing partition splits of sizes `0` and `N - 1` at each recursion step.
options.explanation: If the pivot is always the minimum or maximum element, partitions are maximally unbalanced (`N + (N-1) + ... + 1 = O(N^2)`). Randomized pivot or median-of-three mitigates this.

options.text: When all elements in the array are distinct.
options.explanation: QuickSort thrives on distinct elements with balanced pivots.

options.text: When the array length is an odd number.
options.explanation: Array parity does not affect recursion depth.

options.text: Only when running on single-core processors.
options.explanation: Time complexity is an inherent algorithmic property.

questions.body: What are the worst-case time and auxiliary space complexities of standard MergeSort on an array of size N?
questions.keyPoints: Time: O(N log N), Auxiliary Space: O(N).

options.text: Time: O(N log N), Space: O(N)
options.explanation: MergeSort recursively divides the array into halves (log N depth) and merges sorted subarrays in O(N) time at each level, requiring an auxiliary buffer of size O(N) to hold merged elements.

options.text: Time: O(N log N), Space: O(1)
options.explanation: Standard array merge sort requires O(N) buffer space (in-place array merge sort is complex and slower).

options.text: Time: O(N^2), Space: O(N)
options.explanation: MergeSort guarantees O(N log N) worst-case time.

options.text: Time: O(N), Space: O(log N)
options.explanation: Comparison sorting cannot be faster than O(N log N).

questions.body: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be 'Stable'?
questions.keyPoints: Maintains the relative order of elements that have equal keys.

options.text: Elements with equal keys preserve their original relative order in the sorted output.
options.explanation: A stable sort (like MergeSort or TimSort) guarantees that if item A appears before item B in the input and `key(A) == key(B)`, item A will always appear before item B in the sorted output.

options.text: The algorithm never throws stack overflow exceptions.
options.explanation: Stability refers to equal-key ordering, not memory stability.

options.text: Its running time is identical across all possible inputs.
options.explanation: That describes deterministic time complexity.

options.text: It sorts in-place using O(1) extra memory.
options.explanation: That is the definition of an in-place sort, which is independent of stability.

questions.body: Which of the following statements about HeapSort is true?
questions.keyPoints: O(N log N) guaranteed worst-case, in-place O(1) auxiliary space, NOT stable.

options.text: It guarantees O(N log N) worst-case time, operates in-place with O(1) auxiliary space, but is NOT a stable sort.
options.explanation: HeapSort builds a max-heap in O(N) and repeatedly swaps the root to the end of the array (O(N log N)). It uses O(1) space, but long-distance swaps break stability.

options.text: It is a stable sorting algorithm.
options.explanation: HeapSort is notoriously unstable due to heapify swaps.

options.text: It requires O(N) extra auxiliary memory.
options.explanation: HeapSort organizes the heap directly in the input array in-place.

options.text: Its worst-case time complexity is O(N^2).
options.explanation: HeapSort strictly guarantees O(N log N) worst-case time.

questions.body: What are the time and auxiliary space complexities of Counting Sort for N integers in range `[0, K]`?
questions.keyPoints: Time: O(N + K), Space: O(N + K).

options.text: Time: O(N + K), Space: O(N + K)
options.explanation: Counting sort counts occurrences of each of the `K` distinct values in an array of size `K`, then places elements into an output array in O(N + K) time, bypassing the O(N log N) comparison sort barrier when `K = O(N)`.

options.text: Time: O(N log K), Space: O(1)
options.explanation: Counting sort does not compare elements and requires frequency count space.

options.text: Time: O(N^2), Space: O(K)
options.explanation: Counting sort runs in linear time.

options.text: Time: O(K log N), Space: O(N)
options.explanation: Time is O(N + K).

questions.body: Why must Least Significant Digit (LSD) Radix Sort use a STABLE sorting algorithm (like Counting Sort) as its intermediate subroutine?
questions.keyPoints: Stability preserves the relative sorted order of previous less-significant digits when sorting by more significant digits.

options.text: Stability ensures that sorting by higher-order digits preserves the relative ordering already established by lower-order digits.
options.explanation: If the intermediate sort were unstable, sorting on digit 2 would scramble the order established when sorting on digit 1, producing an incorrect final array.

options.text: Because unstable sorts cannot process numbers in base 10.
options.explanation: Base representation is independent of stability.

options.text: To prevent stack overflow errors during recursion.
options.explanation: LSD Radix sort is typically iterative.

options.text: Because non-stable sorts cannot process strings.
options.explanation: Stability is about preserving previous digit sorting passes.

questions.body: Why can no comparison-based sorting algorithm sort N arbitrary items in faster than `Ω(N log N)` time in the worst case?
questions.keyPoints: A binary decision tree of comparisons has N! permutations as leaves, requiring depth >= log2(N!) = Ω(N log N).

options.text: There are `N!` possible permutations of N elements; a comparison decision tree must have height at least `log2(N!) = Ω(N log N)` to distinguish all permutations.
options.explanation: By Stirling's approximation, `log2(N!) ≈ N log2(N) - N log2(e) = Ω(N log N)`. Since each comparison is a binary branch, the minimum tree depth is Ω(N log N).

options.text: Because memory buses cannot transmit more than N log N bits per second.
options.explanation: The lower bound is an information-theoretic mathematical proof, not hardware bus limits.

options.text: Because CPU clock cycles are limited to logarithmic frequencies.
options.explanation: The limitation is purely algorithmic based on comparisons.

options.text: Because all comparison algorithms use recursion.
options.explanation: Iterative comparison sorts (like iterative heapsort) are also bound by Ω(N log N).

questions.body: What two sorting algorithms are combined in TimSort (the default sorting algorithm in Python, Java, and V8)?
questions.keyPoints: MergeSort and Insertion Sort, optimized for real-world data with existing sorted runs.

options.text: MergeSort and Insertion Sort
options.explanation: TimSort finds natural ordered runs in data and sorts small chunks using Insertion Sort (which has very low overhead and cache locality), then merges runs using an optimized MergeSort algorithm in O(N log N) worst-case and O(N) best-case.

options.text: QuickSort and HeapSort
options.explanation: That combination is IntroSort (used in C++ `std::sort`).

options.text: BubbleSort and Selection Sort
options.explanation: Both are slow O(N^2) algorithms.

options.text: Counting Sort and Radix Sort
options.explanation: Those are non-comparison sorts.

questions.body: What is the average time complexity of QuickSelect (Hoare's selection algorithm) to find the K-th smallest element in an unsorted array?
questions.keyPoints: O(N) average time.

options.text: O(N) average time
options.explanation: Unlike QuickSort which recurses into both partitions (`T(N) = 2T(N/2) + O(N) = O(N log N)`), QuickSelect only recurses into the one partition containing index K: `N + N/2 + N/4 + ... = 2N = O(N)`.

options.text: O(N log N) average time
options.explanation: Sorting the whole array takes O(N log N); QuickSelect finds K-th element in O(N) average.

options.text: O(1) average time
options.explanation: QuickSelect must inspect elements to partition them (linear work).

options.text: O(log N) average time
options.explanation: Logarithmic search requires a pre-sorted array.

questions.body: How can you search for a target value in a sorted array that has been rotated at some unknown pivot in O(log N) time?
questions.keyPoints: Modified binary search: in any rotated sorted array, at least one half (left or right) is always normally sorted.

options.text: On every step, at least one half of the array (`[low..mid]` or `[mid..high]`) is guaranteed to be strictly sorted; check if target falls within the sorted half to determine which direction to branch.
options.explanation: By checking `nums[low] <= nums[mid]`, we identify whether the left half is normally sorted. If target lies in `[nums[low], nums[mid]]`, search left; otherwise search right. This maintains O(log N) complexity.

options.text: Un-rotate the array back to sorted order in O(1) time.
options.explanation: Un-rotating requires shifting elements taking O(N) time.

options.text: Perform linear search because binary search is impossible on rotated arrays.
options.explanation: Modified binary search solves it in O(log N).

options.text: Sort the array with MergeSort first in O(N log N).
options.explanation: Sorting takes O(N log N), which is much slower than direct O(log N) search.

questions.body: How can you find the first and last position of a target value in a sorted array containing duplicates in O(log N) time?
questions.keyPoints: Two separate binary searches: one finding lower bound (first occurrence), one finding upper bound (last occurrence).

options.text: Run two separate binary searches: one that continues searching left when `nums[mid] == target` to find the lower bound, and one that continues searching right to find the upper bound.
options.explanation: When `nums[mid] == target`, instead of returning immediately, recording `ans = mid` and continuing left (`high = mid - 1`) finds the first index. Repeating with rightward branching finds the last index in `2 * O(log N) = O(log N)` total time.

options.text: Find any match via binary search, then expand linearly left and right.
options.explanation: Expanding linearly degrades to O(N) if all elements are identical.

options.text: Binary search cannot handle duplicate elements.
options.explanation: Lower/upper bound binary search handles duplicates cleanly.

options.text: Insert all elements into a hash set.
options.explanation: A hash set takes O(N) space and loses index position information.

questions.body: When does Bucket Sort achieve O(N) average time complexity?
questions.keyPoints: When input numbers are uniformly distributed over a known range.

options.text: When input elements are uniformly distributed over a known interval (e.g. floating point numbers in `[0, 1)`).
options.explanation: When inputs are uniformly distributed, each bucket contains an expected O(1) elements. Sorting each bucket with insertion sort and concatenating takes O(N) total average time.

options.text: When all numbers are powers of 2.
options.explanation: Powers of 2 cluster into few buckets, ruining uniform distribution.

options.text: When the input array is already reverse-sorted.
options.explanation: Sorting reverse-sorted data depends on bucket distribution, not initial order.

options.text: When elements have massive skew and clustering.
options.explanation: If all elements fall into one bucket, bucket sort degrades to O(N^2).

questions.body: How does IntroSort (used in C++ `std::sort`) prevent QuickSort's worst-case O(N^2) degradation?
questions.keyPoints: Starts with QuickSort, switches to HeapSort if recursion depth exceeds 2 * log(N), and uses Insertion Sort for small partitions.

options.text: It monitors QuickSort's recursion depth; if depth exceeds `2 * log(N)`, it switches to HeapSort to guarantee O(N log N) worst-case time, and uses Insertion Sort for small partitions (N < 16).
options.explanation: IntroSort (Introspective Sort) combines QuickSort's practical cache speed with HeapSort's guaranteed O(N log N) worst-case safety net and Insertion Sort's low overhead on tiny arrays.

options.text: It switches to BubbleSort when numbers are negative.
options.explanation: BubbleSort is never used in high-performance standard libraries.

options.text: It runs QuickSort and MergeSort simultaneously on dual CPU cores.
options.explanation: IntroSort is a single-threaded deterministic algorithm.

options.text: It uses random restarts like Simulated Annealing.
options.explanation: It switches deterministically based on recursion call stack depth.

questions.subtopic: Binary Search on Infinite / Unbounded Array
questions.body: How can you search for an element in an unbounded (infinitely long) sorted array where the array length is unknown?
questions.keyPoints: Exponential search: double the window bounds (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) until target <= arr[high], then binary search.

options.text: Exponential Search: start with a window `[0, 1]` and repeatedly double the upper bound (`high *= 2`) until `arr[high] >= target`, then perform binary search within that range.
options.explanation: Exponential search finds the bounding range in O(log P) steps (where P is the target's position), and binary search inside the range takes O(log P), yielding O(log P) total time without knowing array length.

options.text: Scan from index 0 linearly until reaching target.
options.explanation: Linear scan takes O(P) time, which is much slower than O(log P).

options.text: Query `arr[MAX_INT]` immediately.
options.explanation: Index `MAX_INT` might throw an out-of-bounds error or page fault.

options.text: Binary search is impossible without knowing the exact array length.
options.explanation: Exponential search establishes bounds dynamically for binary search.

questions.body: In an array where `nums[i] != nums[i+1]`, how can a peak element (an element strictly greater than its neighbors) be found in O(log N) time?
questions.keyPoints: Binary search: if nums[mid] < nums[mid+1], a peak is guaranteed to exist on the right side.

options.text: Binary search: if `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`, a peak is guaranteed to exist in the right half (`low = mid + 1`); otherwise a peak exists in the left half (`high = mid`).
options.explanation: Because `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`, following the rising slope upwards is guaranteed to eventually hit a peak (at worst the boundary if elements keep rising), allowing logarithmic convergence.

options.text: Scan every element from left to right in O(N) time.
options.explanation: While functional, linear scan is O(N), not the optimal O(log N).

options.text: Sort the array in O(N log N) and return the last element.
options.explanation: Sorting takes O(N log N) and ruins neighbor relationships.

options.text: Calculate the arithmetic derivative across all elements.
options.explanation: That requires O(N) work.

questions.body: What technique is used by database engines to sort a 100 GB dataset on a machine with only 8 GB of RAM?
questions.keyPoints: External Merge Sort: sort chunks in memory, write runs to disk, and merge runs using a K-way min-heap.

options.text: External Merge Sort: divide the file into memory-sized chunks, sort each chunk in RAM and write sorted runs to disk, then merge runs concurrently using a K-way Min-Heap.
options.explanation: External merge sort minimizes disk I/O. Each run fits in RAM. A K-way merge streams the smallest current element across all sorted disk files using a priority queue of size K.

options.text: QuickSort using virtual memory swapping.
options.explanation: Relying on OS virtual memory swapping causes severe disk thrashing and crashes.

options.text: BubbleSort directly on the disk file bytes.
options.explanation: BubbleSort would require billions of random disk seeks.

options.text: Compressing the file with GZIP until it fits in 8 GB RAM.
options.explanation: Compression cannot guarantee arbitrary reduction, and compressed bytes cannot be sorted directly.

questions.body: How can the number of inversions (pairs `(i, j)` where `i < j` but `arr[i] > arr[j]`) in an array be counted in O(N log N) time?
questions.keyPoints: Modified MergeSort: during merge step, if right element is smaller than left element, all remaining left elements form inversions.

options.text: Using a modified MergeSort: during the merge step, whenever an element from the right subarray is picked before an element from the left subarray, it forms inversions with all remaining elements in the left subarray.
options.explanation: Because both halves are sorted, if `arr[j]` from the right half is smaller than `arr[i]` from the left half, `arr[j]` is smaller than all remaining elements `arr[i..mid]`, adding `(mid - i + 1)` inversions in O(N log N) time.

options.text: By checking all pairs with two nested loops in O(N^2).
options.explanation: Brute force takes O(N^2) time.

options.text: By computing the determinant of the array matrix.
options.explanation: Not applicable to 1D inversion counting.

options.text: By running Kadane's algorithm.
options.explanation: Kadane's algorithm finds maximum subarray sum, not inversion count.

questions.body: What is the optimal time complexity to find the median of two sorted arrays of sizes M and N?
questions.keyPoints: O(log(min(M, N))) using binary search on the partition cut of the smaller array.

options.text: O(log(min(M, N)))
options.explanation: By binary searching the partition point in the smaller array such that `max(left_A, left_B) <= min(right_A, right_B)`, the combined median is computed in logarithmic time of the smaller array size.

options.text: O(M + N)
options.explanation: O(M + N) is the two-pointer merge approach, which is suboptimal compared to binary search.

options.text: O((M + N) log(M + N))
options.explanation: Merging and sorting takes O((M + N) log(M + N)).
Constant time is impossible because elements must be partitioned.
